To begin with, I think it is only appropriate that I admit to being a fairly avid reader of John Sandford over the years, especially a fan of his Lucas Davenport “Prey” series. A pretty big fan to be honest. That is until the last couple of years… Now that fanship is struggling… When we last saw our fearless hero, Lucas Davenport, he was still recovering from being shot during a shootout with bad guys in his federal marshal job. When this book begins, Lucas has been called to Washington, DC to meet with Elmer Henderson and Porter Smalls, two U.S. Senators from Minnesota who have used him several times to conduct investigations in his home state, as well as playing key roles Audrey Coil, the rebellious teenage daughter of a U.S. Senator has been busy building up her social media presence. While promoting her blog videos she ends up finding her own picture of on a very strange website titled “1919” that references articles and propaganda from several Neo-Nazi and other radical hate groups. And it gets worse, because there are more pictures of other children of politicians identified by their name. Lucas is charged with investigating whether the website is serving to call out extremists to attack the loved ones of powerful Washington, DC politicians with deadly intent? Lucas is given an FBI focal, Jane Chase, who he has worked with before, as a resource. Lucas also calls in has two federal Marshall agents – Bob and Rae - both of whom are witty, hard-working and never lack an opinion. However, trying to find some a killer willing to eliminate children among violent anti-government hate groups while the clock is running is looking like an impossible task, even for Lucas. There are a couple of good things in this novel – Lucas going hunting and having Bob and Rae around – everything else was sadly disappointing. It hurts my fanship deeply to share the following criticisms: - This book is way too political; it is way over the top with political references of all kind. There were so many of them, including comments about left-wing, right wing, National Socialism, White Supremacy, hate groups, anti-government organizations, Neo-Nazi, gun control, Democrat vs. Republican, CNN vs. Fox talk shows, abortion, rape, and Trump. Too much time was spent on this rhetoric than investing in a compelling and interesting story. - There are no strong bad guys. No devious serial killers. No evil plotting adversaries worthy of Davenport’s attention. The one primary villain is extremely weak, experiencing his first kill, and carries no sense of challenge for anyone. He is by far the weakest opponent Lucas has ever faced. - There is very little interaction with Weather and none with his daughter in college, who is completely absent from the pages. - Nothing much of any substance happens in the first half of the book. The action doesn’t even start until page 208 (out of a 406-page book). It took so long to get moving that I actually jotted down the page number when the story kicked into gear. - The last 100 pages (25% of the book) is one large and over-extended chase scene to capture the weak killer. You know the ending before it happens because it is much too predictable. Over the last four years, Sandford’s quality has really slowed down. 2017’s “Golden Prey” and last year’s “Neon Prey” both suffered from a one-dimensional, weak plotting. Now this year’s “Masked Prey” is a an even feebler read than those two were. Sandford can tell as story well, but the truth is three of his last four books have not been good stories. They were not interesting, nor complex. They lacked strong adversaries for Lucas and complex plotting. The didn’t have layered storylines that stretched Davenport’s character and intellect. Quite frankly, they were weak and lacked Sandford’s writing style that was once fast-paced, fluid, and sharp, seems more now like a stream of consciousness – one that rambles and is extremely disjointed at times. Overall, to be transparent and completely honest, I found this to be Sanderson’s weakest outing for Lucas Davenport. I am not sure how he went off the rails in three of his last four books, but I am hoping that we haven’t seen the last of Lucas at his best. Here’s hoping that the next outing will include a reinvigorating storyline rather than another lazy, mailed-in lackluster story. Come on John, let’s get it turned around… And sooner rather than later. My fandom is struggling to keep interest…

From what I have gathered, Elin Hilderbrand novels perfectly capture the spirit of a summer read. What "summer read" actually means, I'm not too sure. This was my first time reading a Hilderbrand novel. I've seen some of her other works in the past and riffled through pages while considering a purchase, but I've never actually read them. However, after reading review after review extolling this book, I thought, "Why not?" and bought the book. My thoughts on the book follow; there will be some spoilers so please proceed with caution. --------- I'll be blunt; it's a fairly mediocre book. It centers around Lizbet Keaton, a newly single woman whose relationship with JJ (her ex) was forever ruined when Lizbet discovered salacious text messages from JJ to another woman. Lizbet used to run a restaurant with JJ called The Deck, but after their relationship crashed Lizbet needs some space and decides to find a new job. That new job ends up being the general manager position for a newly renovated hotel. Billionaire entrepreneur Xavier Darling has decided to purchase the Hotel Nantucket, a dilapidated and haunted (that's right, haunted) old hotel. The hotel is haunted by the ghost of Grace Hadley, a 19-year-old maid from the early 1900s who was having an affair with the owner. The owner's wife, Dahlia, was apparently quite a vicious and nasty woman. Dahlia decided that she wanted to get rid of Grace, and we find out at the very end of the book through a journal confirmation that has suddenly been discovered that Dahlia set fire to the hotel and locked Grace in her room. Grace spends the novel spying on everyone. She is simultaneously invisible and corporeal, since she can apparently wear a bathrobe and cap and exert force on wrongdoers. Let's go through the cast of characters: Lizbet Keaton is the main character of the story. She is trying to move on with her life. She ends up falling in love with Mario Subiaco, who just happens to be incredibly attractive and an incredibly talented chef. Oh, Mario is also JJ's (Lizbet's cheating ex) idol. Kimber is a woman who comes to spend the summer at the hotel with her two kids and dog. Her son Louie loves chess and beats absolutely everybody who plays against him. Her daughter Wanda loves exploring the hotel, somehow discovers that Grace is a ghost in the hotel and writes an article about the ghost that goes viral and spurs the reputation of the Hotel Nantucket. At the end, we discover that Kimber is also the incredibly famous and anonymous hotel reviewer who goes by the name Shelly Carpenter. Edie is a young woman who works at the front desk of the hotel and is being blackmailed by her ex who is using indelicate videos that he coerced her into participating in. She's generally a good person. Alessandra is an attractive woman who seduces wealthy married gentlemen and blackmails them into giving her money. She also works at the front desk. She does some pretty questionable things throughout the novel. For example, she sleeps with a man named Michael Bick. They seem to have a great time, although Michael is obviously cheating on his wife. When she leaves, she blackmails Michael into giving her $50,000 and then still plants evidence in the house so that when Michael's wife, Heidi, returns, she will suspect that Michael is in fact having an affair with their close friend and neighbor. Chad is a young man from a very wealthy family who partied a lot and screwed up big time (partially blinded his friend, let his family's house where he was throwing a party burn down, and let his family dog die). Chad is on a redemption arc by working as a maid at the Hotel Nantucket for the summer. Magda is the head maid who just so happens to be the person who Xavier Darling has been in love with for 30+ years. She's also absurdly rich because she made a lucky bet (with her own money, as was repeated several times) and invested her winnings with Xavier. There are a number of other ancillary characters, but quite frankly I don't want to go through all of them. It doesn't really matter. This is a book to read if you enjoy gossip. There isn't really any major conflict in this novel. The primary plot point is that Lizbet desperately wants to get a 5 key (star) review from an anonymous hotel critic. Keep in mind that all of this happens on Nantucket Island, so everyone is in everyone else's business. That's pretty much it. Reading the book, I never felt that any of the characters would not be okay at the end. There is no sense of danger or struggle, just a bunch of bland characters thrown together for a summer in a feel-good novel that goes nowhere. I was not a fan of the ghost. I did not care for many of the characters. Most importantly, the book unfortunately was not especially engaging. Another novel that I've read, A Gentleman in Moscow, follows the same general theme of this novel. In A Gentleman in Moscow the main character is of course imprisoned in the hotel, but the idea is that we as readers become attached to the main character and the ragtag group of people who work at the hotel and who the main character befriends. As in this novel, I didn't feel much of a sense of fear for the characters. However, A Gentleman in Moscow was quite simply a better written novel. I cared for the characters more, the plot spanned much more time, and the language was elegant and at times beautiful. This book was not terrible. Sadly, in my opinion it was certainly not great either. It focused too much on drama and superficial romantic plot points. It's a light read, and based on the reviews, other people are clearly enjoying the book. While I'm surprised at the intense positive feedback, I'm glad that other people are enjoying the novel. It was only ok for me, but it may be good for you. At least I tried it out; always try new things!

I was really feeling fortunate to have an opportunity to read best-selling author John Grisham’s latest legal thriller, thanks to Netgalley.com. Unfortunately the book did not live up to my expectations for a number of reasons. The third and final volume starring defense lawyer Jake Brigance starts off powerfully as we are plunged into the death of a blind-drunk abusive police officer by one of his terrified victims. The setting is the same sleepy, insular stereotyped Mississippi community we have experienced before, peopled with ignorant bigots, a few colorful characters with good hearts and our hero Jake. Unfortunately as soon as Jake shows up in the story the drama is dialed back. As usual, Jake wants no part in taking on the defense of the accused, the traumatized adolescent son of a woman who was the victim of frequent domestic violence at the hands of the now dead cop, Stu Kofer. Jake is still suffering money problems and hasn’t overcome the horrors he faced from local enemies as a result of his previous big court victory. The prospect of having to defend the killer of a police officer with a stellar reputation understandably brings back all of Jake’s anxiety and fears, but his mentor, the judge in the case, applies pressure and Jake reluctantly takes the case. Grisham now goes into formula mode. Every chapter is padded with paragraphs about such minutia as Jake’s healthy breakfast choices and descriptions of daily routines that add pages but not value to the story. The worst example though is his course in Courtroom 101. Since this is the third in a legal series it seems fair to assume most of his readers will know the basics of courtroom procedure. The addition of all this superfluous explanation slows down the story and condescends to Grisham’s readers. The best part of any legal thriller is, of course, the questioning of the witnesses and seeing the strategy of the lawyers unfold. Perry Mason used to do this every week when he delighted his viewers with a surprise that confounded Hamilton Burger and won the day. Well, there was a surprise in this story too, but the reader learns it early on, and the only question is when Jake is going to spring it on the prosecution. And if you are looking for a powerful ending that ties up all the loose ends and sends Jake happily into the sunset, I’m afraid you are going to be disappointed. Frankly I think Grisham was tired of Jake. The writer must have had a three book deal to tell Jake’s story, but really he didn’t seem worth the effort. There was no passion in the man, little humor and not even much personal struggle, except for the constant worry about paying his bills. I’ve got a suggestion if he ever feels tempted to write about Jake again. Relocate him from this caricature of a sleepy southern town and let him be a real lawyer.

I keep reading John Grisham’s books, but sadly, I can only recommend his very early books. And the icing on the cake for this so-so book was the author’s note at the end. Basically he says that he’s too lazy to make sure that all the laws he’s writing about, are in fact, correct. What? That’s not just lazy, but in my opinion, disrespectful of the legions of readers who have put him up on the pedestal he sits on today.

In a small-town university in Quebec, a notorious mathematician/statistician (notorious not being a typical adjective for such people) is due to give a talk between Christmas and New Year. So much, so bland, you might be thinking. The problem is that this statistician has a very unpalatable position on how to avoid future pandemics - by the involuntary euthanasia of the elderly, sick and disabled. Her talk draws opposing crowds and leads to an attempted murder. Chief Inspector Gamache is working security during the talk and soon trying to work out how the gun got into the university hall, and how a person connected with the speaker gets murdered a couple of days later. I am surprised at how highly rated this book is. Not that I can see no reason why readers might like it— I can —but it does not come across as a crowd-pleaser. Had I read this book before it became a hit, I would have expected it to be divisive. The reason being that it's hard to explain or categorise this story. It is a very strange literary book, built of components— some I liked, a lot I didn’t— that didn’t really add up to a cohesive whole. Is it a satire? It seems it must be because some parts are obviously intended to be funny. Humour is highly-subjective and, I have to admit, most of this wasn't my particular flavour. Very over-the-top goofy humour at times. The story reimagines Mark Twain's Jim-- a character who is treated as benign and a bit simple-minded --as a secret intellectual who can not only read, but is well-versed in Voltaire. In this version, the way Black slaves behave and speak is not their true selves but a performance for slave owners. I tried my best to get on board with this, because there is something quite amusing and satisfying about an author taking the way slavers belittled, stereotyped and made jokes about slaves, and being like ha, joke's on you. But, then, other parts are aggressively unfunny. Floggings, lynchings and an on-page rape. I remember thinking at one point: Is this the point? Is Everett just that clever? Was he waiting for the reader to have the audacity to laugh before screaming “Oh so you think this shit is funny, do you?! Well, here’s a woman being raped.”? I just don’t know. And, by the way, I do not think every book needs to have central female characters, but I do think you have a responsibility not to introduce female characters for the sole purpose of them being rape victims. Especially when there are already almost no women of note in the book. I found the decisions Everett made here curious… he rewrites a character who I agree needed rewriting, but I expected a complex character, someone with depth of characterisation… it is strange to me, and a bit farcical, that Everett replaces the stereotyped, one-dimensional Jim we know with another surface level character whose entire personality seems to be "secret genius." Everett's Jim plays a rough-talking halfwit to his white overlords but secretly has dream conversations with Voltaire and Locke. Other than this satirical twist that actually Jim was a genius, I didn’t feel we knew him at all. And: “Are you referring to my diction or my content?” is a line a robot would say, not a closeted intellectual. Then there's the plot itself, the style of which is very much just the characters running from one place and drama to the next. It reads like a series of sketches, some comedic, some horrific, with a twist that I am still undecided about. Knowledge of the characters and general story in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is pretty much necessary for the book's events to have significance. So, again, I'm surprised this book has been as universally-loved as it seems to have been. A rating above 4.5 at more than 200,000 ratings is impressive, so I guess I'm the problem.

The Wish is a rightwing conservative morality tale in the vein of Karen Kingsbury’s Someone Like You in which author Nicholas Sparks appropriates a pregnant teen girl’s experience from the perspective of a middle age white male. Protagonist Maggie starts out as a desperate teen mother and ends up as a dying cancer victim. When she finds out she’s pregnant, abortion is villified, single motherhood is averted, and adoption is praised as the only “virtuous” option. Frumpy, lackadaisical, low-achieving Maggie is juxtaposed with male counterparts Bryce and Mark--physically, intellectually, and morally muscular--unrealistically flawless “saviors.” “I was pretty clueless about the state of the world...and honestly didn’t care all that much. But I liked hearing him talk and he occasionally posed serious questions about serious issues. After pretending to think about it, I’d say something like, ‘That’s difficult to answer. What do you think?’ and he’d start explaining his thoughts on the matter...I’d enjoyed the sight of his muscles...It made me wish that I could be more like him.” The novel wraps up with a saccharine and predictable reunion tied with the bow of Maggie’s last words to Mark, “Thank you for finding me and becoming my wish somehow made true.” If you “wish” for a more authentic alternative, Jennifer Weiner’s That Summer is a similarly setting-based novel that tackles parallel issues with diverse characters and depth of perspective. While Sparks’ “reckoning” is the impending birth of Maggie’s baby and departure from Bryce, Weiner describes, “This is a reckoning...if I sit here and do nothing, I’m...complicit...‘Do you think you deserved what happened to you that summer?’...No girl did...I don’t think it’s about blame. It’s about what happens next….All the girls who come after us.”

When I first began reading this book, I was delighted at the feeling of being enveloped in this dark, Grimm Fairy Tale type place called Oz. The concept of the time dragon, the dwarf-operated marionette machine completely spooked me. The baby elphaba with her green skin and huge teeth was freakish, yet I could feel a tenderness at her otherness, the trouble she would surely find fitting in. From then on, the book became much less interesting or sympathetic. Elphaba never morphed into a likable character. I genuinely did not like her and did not care about her fate, problematic as she is the main character. It is apparent that Maguire is trying to dehumanize her in the latter part of the book, referring to her as "witch" rather than "Elphaba." But even in her formative college years, she is unlikable and condescending. From a dialogue perspective, Maguire attempts to make her witty at times, but she is not witty at all. She is an awkward conversationalist, yet always shares her snide opinions. From here, Elphaba becomes a terrorist for the greater good of helping Animals. The flaws of terrorism -- the way Elphaba shrugs off how innocents will die as necessary to the greater good makes me very unsympathetic to her cause. I feel she should be wiser, smarter, cleverer than that -- and she's not. But the real reason to dislike Elphaba is the treatment of what is surely her own son. She treats him coldly, like a servant and offers no parenting to him at all. She is so indifferent, she cares more for her bees and crows and monkeys with wings. Perhaps, Elphaba is really not very human. You would think that Maguire would show that underneath her physical deformities is a sensitive human with great intelligence and abilities. I see a subhuman with a crabby negative demeanor that gets her nowhere. Maybe I'm not getting the political or philosophical commentary. Maybe I'm not seeing how Elphaba needs to be this way to make the book work. But in my view, a book will never work if there isn't a solitary character to like and emphathize with. And there wasn't. My recommendation to anyone: see the musical -- for all its cliches, it's a much more satisfying experience.

Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets is yet another global romp through the corridors of history, symbolism, and questionable geography. The plot, if you can call it that, unfolds like a fever dream stitched together by someone who fell asleep during a History Channel marathon. Does it make sense? Absolutely not. But since when has “making sense” been a requirement for a Dan Brown novel? Reality in this book is more like an optional suggestion, loosely waved at before the characters sprint off to the next set piece. The pacing is relentless - mostly because if you stopped to think about the logic for more than three seconds, you’d burst out laughing. For example, when Langdon ran back to his hotel, pulled the fire alarm, and then jumped into an icy lake - all because his faulty extrasensory perception picked up the “whiff of death” - you realize you’re no longer reading a thriller, you’re watching a Monty Python sketch that accidentally took itself seriously And yet, somehow, the man remains one of the most widely read authors on the planet. How? I have no idea. Literary critics might call his prose clunky, his dialogue wooden, and his metaphors criminal, but apparently, millions of readers call it “a page-turner.” Maybe that’s the real secret of secrets. I give it 2 stars out of 5 - one star for the energy, 1/2 a star for the occasional moment of actual suspense, and 1/2 a star just because I admire the sheer audacity of making this nonsense a (possible *yawn) global best-seller. If there’s a lesson here, it’s this: Dan Brown is the perfect poster child for every struggling writer. If this can top charts, then by all means, keep writing. Because if Dan Brown can become a publishing phenomenon with labyrinths of gibberish dressed up as profound insight, then honestly- so can you.

Windsor Horne Lockwood III – a dubious antihero with very personal visions of justice and the fine distinctions between legality and morality Arising out of Harlan Coben’s Myron Bolitar universe, Windsor Horne Lockwood III is a mythical near superhero, operating with the guidance of his own moral compass and very personal distinctions between right and wrong. He is willing to spend his vast wealth and exert his talents for violence, murder and mayhem however he sees fit to make his will and decisions come to pass in a manner that recalls Edward Woodward’s 1985 portrayal of THE EQUALIZER. With WIN, author Coben brings WHL III out of the shadows and showcases him operating on his own behalf – recovering a pair of priceless Vermeer and Picasso paintings belong to his family, solving a murder in which that family is implicated because his suitcase was recovered in the murder victim’s apartment, and dealing with the 21st century resolution of a decades old mystery of domestic terrorism dating as far back as the Kent State mass murders and the ironically violent peace protests against the US involvement in the Vietnam War! Win is not a likable protagonist, not that he cares what anyone thinks about him. The only opinion that matters to him is his own. Consider this brief autobiography that he offers in his own words: “I grew up in privilege … every human being is snap-judged by their looks. … the fact is, many people detest me on sight. They see the towheaded blond locks, the ruddy complexion, the porcelain features, my haughty resting face – they smell the inescapable stink of old money that comes off me in relentless waves – and they think smug, snob, elitist, lazy, judgmental, undeservedly wealthy ne’er-do-good who was born not only with a silver spoon in his mouth but with a forty-eight-piece silver place setting with a side of titanium steak knives.” “… I understand this. I, too, sometimes feel that way about those who inhabit my socioeconomic sphere …” “… I had the financial means, the motivation, the past trauma, the innate skills, the disposition, and perhaps, when I am most honest with myself, some sort of loose screw (or primitive survival mechanism?) that allows me to not only thrive but take some pleasure from acts of violence.” So, what does a reader take away from that? Well, this reader sees a protagonist that is narcissistic, self-righteous, and self-serving, violent (pathologically so) and very unlikable. The story, once again in this reader’s sole opinion, is not terribly credible AND I look askance at Coben’s portrayal of the abilities of the legitimate police force who seem to have totally forgotten that Win did commit murders in the solution of the crime in question!! What’s up with that? Do they just get swept under the rug and ignored? I’ll carry on with the Myron Bolitar series, hope that my opinion doesn’t ruin a perfectly good MB series novel in which Win makes an appearance, and definitely forego any future novels in the Windsor Horne Lockwood III series. Not recommended. Paul Weiss

Praying this was ghostwritten. ___________________________________ Some Thoughts™️ I'm willing to throw hands to defend Kaladin's place as one of the best characters ever written. That said, his therapist arc is trash—as is much of this book. Each of the main characters in Stormlight suffers internally: Kaladin has depression, Shallan has dissociative identity disorder, Dalinar is an alcoholic, Renarin is on the autism spectrum, Adolin has daddy issues, Navani is insecure, and Jasnah is self-absorbed. Most of them also experience symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. The Stormlight Archive has, historically, dealt with these issues in an empathetic and hopeful manner, while managing to keep the external conflicts of Roshar at the forefront of the narrative. In The Way of Kings, Kaladin finds the strength to live despite his pain; he also kills a Shardbearer, forms and trains Bridge Four, and saves Dalinar and Adolin. In Words of Radiance, Shallan's identity fractures and she learns to accept herself; she also survives a shipwreck, crosses a continent unaided, secures a marriage alliance, works for the Ghostbloods, travels the chasms, and discovers Urithiru. Wind and Truth, unfortunately, smushes plot, conflict, and subtlety in the mud. The only characters really doing anything are Szeth and Adolin, and each of their plotlines is more repetitive than Navani's internal dialogue in Rhythm of War. Adolin is my homeboy, but his entire POV in Wind and Truth is 1) fight impossible battle, 2) think about daddy issues, 3) play towers with Yanagawn. Szeth's POV, on the other hand, reads like the training course in Call of Duty: Kill an Honorbearer in a temple, kill an Honorbearer in your dreams, kill an Honorbearer with your powers, kill an Honorbearer with your sword . . . . Shallan, Renarin, Rlain, Navani, and Dalinar spend the whole book floating in the Spiritual Realm to provide an unwanted history lesson. Jasnah continues to think about herself. Sigzil is drained of all personality and placed as a prop to make us, again, hate Moash. Kaladin plays the flute and obsesses over whether he can perform life-changing therapy in ten days—and for some reason, he can? three times? Speaking of Kaladin, Sanderson would have to wear Thanos's gauntlet to be any more heavyhanded. (Marvel referenced with purpose; see Adolin's, (view spoiler)) Nothing made me miss the warm camaraderie of Bridge Four like Wind and Truth. I missed laughter around the fire, sweat over months of training, bonds forged through communal mourning. Bridge Four restored so many men because each learned, in his own unique time and way, that he wasn't alone. Slowly, bridge run after bridge run, these men found the courage to hope again. To believe in something bigger than one bridge crew. That maybe each of them, through small actions, could make the world just a bit better. In Wind and Truth, Sanderson bulldozed the quiet healing of Bridge Four with graceless authorial insertions. The reader was not asked to realize, with some afterthought, how far their beloved characters had come. Readers were told, like the outro of a 2000s Disney movie, exactly what healing had taken place, and why, and that they too should consider therapy. I'm not unhappy that Stormlight's cast of characters underwent some much-needed therapy. I just protest my need to witness 1,300 pages of it. Especially when those 1,300 pages read something like this: "I believe in you," Vienta whispered. "I . . . believe in us, Sigzil. We're what they want, for once." "Live this truth," he said. I will admit, though, that where Wind and Truth ends has my interest piqued. Assuming Sanderson gets an editor (yes, I know he has many, I just don't know what editing is taking place), I'd like to read the rest of the series. I maintain, however, that Wind and Truth could have been one paragraph long: (view spoiler) This approach lacks nuance, but so does Wind and Truth.

1.75/5🌟 Spoiler Free First of all, I want to start off by saying if you loved this book, I am so happy for you. Keep loving it! Unfortunately, I did not and had to fight for my life not to dnf it. I’m going to break this down into categories to give y’all an idea of why, for me, W&T is far more than a bad Stormlight book, it’s one of the worst fantasy books I’ve read in recent memory. Prose - Sanderson has never been known for having strong prose but my god, has the quality dropped significantly. It felt like the book was constantly talking down to me. Repeating the same info from 6 different povs, 20 chapters in a row. The use of modern language took me right out of the story, and the dialogue was nearly unreadable at times with a strong YA vibe that had no business being in an adult fantasy epic. For me, W&T read like the fanfiction of a 14yr old SA fan with a DSM-5. Pacing - The amount of nothing. This word count is absurd. If you cut out the middle, slammed the beginning and end together, you’d be able to figure out what’s happening. This book is almost entirely filler, with nothing of value to add to the arcs or the plot. World building - Is it cool? I guess, but it doesn’t matter. What you learn has no bearing on the story. For a series that prides itself on “Journey before destination” there is a severe lack of actual journey. Sanderson breaks his own magic rules for plot, and sacrifices logic for moving the story along. Everything about the Spiritual Realm fills me with rage. How does it work? When the author wants it to. Arcs - The kumbaya of it all. Why is everyone suddenly so unrealistically self aware? I should be punching my fist into the air. I should be inconsolable with grief, yet I feel absolutely nothing. Adolin was the only pov I actively enjoyed. The snap of this man’s back carrying W&T echos. These characters felt nothing like the people I’ve grown to know and love. There were fundamental technical writing skills, outside of storytelling, that I had issue with here. I’m glad Sanderson isn’t writing another SA book for some years, I need that long a distance to decide whether I’ll pick up book 6 or not.

Ever since The Way of Kings, I regarded Brandon as, perhaps, the brightest modern fantasy writer. Yes, he's not Martin with his encyclopedic knowledge of history and impeccable talent for writing smart characters, and not Rothfuss either, since Brandon's writing doesn't come near enough to his poetic charm, and definitely not as fresh and almost revolutionary to the genre as Abercrombie. Still, the scope of Sanderson's body of work is so ambitious that it hides his flaws behind the sheer scale of enormity and, the most important of all, sincerity. The first two Stormlight books were brilliant. I instantly adored Roshar, appreciated how unfamiliar and alien it was, and enjoyed slowly understanding the rules and principles behind this land and its societies. The Way of Kings was much more ambitious than Mistborn and all of its derivatives, and it made so many promises of mystery and novelty that I was instantly hooked. Words of Radiance expanded upon it, adding even more of what made the first book great. Oathbringer was good but not as great, though still, it was only a middle point! RoW was where everything started to fall apart. As the penultimate parts often are, it was tense and right on the edge of giving all the answers Wind and Truth should've provided. Still, I feel like Brandon got too excited about writing and explaining a "complex magic system"®, which got in the way of the story itself. The book turned out to be half misery and suffering and another half a weird combination of natural philosophy with fantasy mumbo-jumbo. The final book is underwhelming. Maybe it's my fault, as I had too many expectations. Journey before the destination and all that. And yet, I can't shake off the feeling that Stormlight started as the most fresh, original, and exciting fantasy book series of the 21st century and ended like a season 5 of a mediocre TV show from the CW - on a really annoying cliffhanger, full of too-modern-to-be-immersive jokes, and, worst of all, confusing mental disorders with personality traits. But these would be forgivable if not for the book's biggest problem: it's oversaturation. There's too much of EVERYTHING - from the number of characters to their overflowing emotion, from forced romance plots to connections with other Cosmere books - what once was a fun nod to other stories, connecting them into one universe, now became an annoying reminder about how much the Cosmere changed in recent years, as to follow the plot of this book one needs to read about 10 to 15 other ones from Sanderson, and this is just too much commitment to a single author, in my opinion. And don't get me started on an overabundance of everything magical - light, voidlight, anti-light, anti-voidlight, but wait, there's more! The lowest point of the book comes right near the end, where a particular character gets asked who they are, and they respond, "Well, I guess I'm a therapist." It was the single most immersion-breaking thing I ever expected to read, almost akin to screaming, "Hey, it's a JOKE! In my HIT BOOK SERIES, THE STORMLIGHT ARCHIVE! THERAPIST, LIKE IN THE REAL WORLD, Y'KNOW?" It just came off as... cheap. I felt the same after The Lost Metal. Like the Cosmere is collapsing on itself. And Wind and Truth, unfortunately, confirmed this. There's too much and too many - worlds, interconnected and overarching plots, characters, and magic systems, and I feel like because of that overabundance, because of interconnectivity, the present, here and now, isn't getting enough time, energy, and story relevance to pull off a satisfying conclusion, everything should always be about one more mystery, one more story, about references and implication, and it just became... boring. At one point, I figured that if anyone could pull this gargantuan project of dozens of books connecting into one story off, it would be Brandon, but it seems the ambition was too much for one man, sorry. I think after Wind and Truth, the series (and the universe) is only at half-point, but I'm done.

This is my first Emily Henry book that turned out being such a letdown for me, as I was a big fan of the rest of her stories, or at least most of them. I'm still not entirely sure if the title was meant to refer to the way our two main characters, Miles and Daphne, began their relationship—"You know, Funny Story.. my fiancé dumped me for his childhood best friend, who happened to be Miles’s girlfriend, and that’s how we ended up living together, and then I accidentally told my ex-fiancé that Miles and I are dating, so now we are fake dating.", or if it was just meant to suggest that this would be a fun story to read. I actually loved that she stood her ground and never considered going back to her cheating ex-fiancé, unlike our hero who wasn't so sure about it and who, speaking of which—let's get to him now. Miles Nowak, our Bridget Jones's Diary-watching, spicy-woodsy-smelling (like every other romance book hero), Crocs-loving hero who as for now is my least favorite Emily Henry male character. The love of your life? Hell no. I didn't like that he said that about his cheating ex-girlfriend, so I expected him to say the same thing about the heroine later in the book, but that didn't happen. I know he loved Daphne and chose her, but this quote left a bitter taste in my mouth. Or when the question was asked "if they would get back together with their exes" and Daphne's answer was this "Would he take her back? I find myself wondering, before seamlessly transitioning into Would I take Peter back? “Definitely not,” I say aloud." and Miles’s that "Petra was the exception, not the rule, for me. What do you mean "I don’t know."?? It should have been "No." from the very beginning when you found out about it. The worst moment in the book that confirmed me why he is my least favorite Emily Henry hero was when he went to see his ex when she called him crying and because of that he left Daphne waiting for him. "And then Petra called, and she was sobbing. So hard I couldn’t understand her. I’d never seen her cry before. I honestly thought someone had died. She asked if I could come see her, and I said yes. "I didn’t mean to tell her first.” The tops of his cheeks redden. “That I’m in love with you." And then the first person to know he loved Daphne was also his ex. You know that feeling when you read a romance novel and you just feel that the hero loves the heroine? In Miles' case it was the opposite. Throughout the book, I had the impression that if his ex-girlfriend wanted to come back to him, he would welcome her with open arms. Only at the end of the book, when he did one thing, I was like "Hmm, okay, maybe he loves Daphne then.". But as I just said, I only started feeling it at the end of the book. All the things I mentioned, plus the fact that a month after the breakup he still kept pictures of her in his room instead of burning them, are why he will probably always be my least favorite Emily character. I don't even know what to say about the romance part of the book because it was boring as the chemistry between Daphne and Miles seemed non-existent to me. They finally confessed their love to each other, and the only thing I felt was happiness, because I knew that this book would end soon. I guess that alone says enough how much I enjoyed their love story. I never expected that reading Emily Henry's book would evoke so many unpleasant emotions in me, and yet, as you can see, it unfortunately happened. ★ 2.75 stars i guess it’s time for me to start considering that maybe i’m not exactly the target audience for Emily Henry’s books. see, i don’t think she’s a bad author. i really don’t. believe it or not, i do think she’s a good writer and i can understand (to a certain extent) why most people are obsessed with her work. but as much as i tried and keep trying, i can’t be one of those people. aside from this book, i’ve read four other books by EH. you can easily guess which ones because they are her most popular: Beach Read, Book Lovers, People We Meet On Vacation and Happy Place. i hated Book Lovers & PWMOV, but enjoyed Beach Read and Happy Place [she’s very hit or miss as you can notice]. however, while these two books were enjoyable — back when i read them, at least — i can’t exactly say i was obsessed with them. were they good? well, yes, but they weren’t perfect and i personally found them a bit overhyped. my not-so-extraordinary experiences with her past works were the main reason why i didn’t have high expectations for Funny Story. although, deep down, i wanted it to be the book that would make me say “wow... now i really understand all the hype she gets, i’m definitely an Emily Henry fan now!” but that obviously did not happen. it’s such a shame because this book actually started off good. i mean... kind of. in the first 50% i was convinced that this was going to be a 3 star read — i know people have different thoughts about three star ratings; some think it’s reserved for bad reads, others think it’s reversed for decent/‘just okay’ reads. in my opinion, it can mean both, it just depends on the book. at first, i thought Funny Story would be getting the “decent/‘just okay’ three star rating” from me. i was liking some things, but disliking others. our female main character, Daphne Vincent, was one of the things i was liking. she was imperfect and flawed, but also realistic, which was a nice thing to me. i prefer reading stories with characters who are not perfect and have flaws because that makes them feel more human, real, and easy to relate with. of course there were particular things i didn’t like about her and i won’t lie that sometimes throughout the book i found myself getting annoyed at her, but generally speaking, Daphne was not an awful character. not the most remarkable or loveable if we’re being brutally honest — i do wish Emily had given her a more captivating personality, but she was still likeable despite that so i’m not going to complain much. my favorite thing about her character is probably the fact that she is a librarian, how cool is that? she’s living the dream! as for our male main character, Miles Nowak... um, was i supposed to care about him? because i didn’t, sorry. honestly, Miles is not even a bad MMC and i truly had nothing against him — the thing is that i just found him uninteresting and rather forgettable. sure, he was cool guy occasionally and he had a few nice moments, but that’s about it. nothing more to tell you. Miles didn’t have any outstanding or charming qualities in my opinion and i was pretty indifferent about him for the majority of the book. i thought he would win me over eventually, but eh, he never did. the story itself was not the bestest and most interesting i’ve ever read, but the positive thing is that it was keeping me somewhat entertained. even with its issues, i was not bored and i wanted to keep reading more and more. i even started feeling a tad hopeful that things would improve at some point because i could see some potential there. but guess what? it did not improve. in fact, it got worse. i don’t know where exactly things started going wrong, all i can tell you is that after 50% i lost all my interest in the story. i assume it might be because of the romance. Daphne and Miles started having more “romantic” scenes and i was not interested in that. not even a little bit. from the beginning, i couldn’t feel any chemistry between them and their romantic interactions were all so cringe and unnatural to me. just unpleasing to read. so yeah, it actually makes sense why i lost interest when they really started becoming more than friends. i genuinely enjoyed the friendship between these two, their dynamic as friends was fun and sweet, but as a couple? oh, absolutely NOT. when i read romance books i surely expect to root for the main characters to end up together, because duh, but Funny Story made me do the exact opposite. Daphne and Miles should’ve stayed as friends and friends only and i’ll die on this hill. no one can convince me otherwise. it’s not even just because i think they have zero chemistry, there are another million reasons why i think that that they shouldn’t be a couple. the biggest one is that neither of them were very prepared to embark in another serious relationship so quickly (nor they should). they should take care of themselves first and get therapy instead. on top of that, the author also started coming up with unnecessary and tedious subplots. like for example the dad subplot — the most boring — and i just... couldn’t take it anymore. i was getting more and more annoyed and the urge to give up was very strong at that point, but i kept pushing through. i don’t know why, though? it wasn’t even worth it. then... when i thought it couldn’t get any worse... the author throws in a ✨ third act conflict ✨ and what a stupid, irritating third act conflict it was. was it even necessary? it came out of nowhere and the whole thing felt way too forced and annoying. (view spoiler) ironically, for a book called Funny Story, this wasn’t funny at all. it’s not the worst book i’ve ever read (trust me when i say i’ve read worse) but it’s not one of the best either... it was just not for me i guess. i still recommend it, though — i feel like others might like it more than me. i certainly hope they do. 𓂃 ⚝ 𓂃 ๋. ₊ ꒰ ✉️ favorite quotes. ꒱ ₊ . ๋ 𓂃 ⚝ 𓂃 “The same universe that dispassionately takes things away can bring you things you weren't imaginative enough to dream up.” “You can’t untell someone your secrets. all i am going to say for now is that i am disappointed.

I’m really bummed out by this trend in YA and Chick-Lit novels where once-perfect characters are now portrayed as flawed individuals with substance abuse issues, all to fit into a modern, ‘progressive’ world. Sure, the main characters still have chemistry, but the overall plot feels shallow and lacks excitement. It’s like Emily Henry is more focused on crafting a trendy, relatable image than on delivering a compelling story. Maybe I’m just too old for this stuff. Even when I’m in the mood for a quick, easy read, the constant rehashing of the same themes is a total turn-off. The story’s premise is pretty basic: the protagonist ends up with his ex-fiancé’s current girlfriend’s ex-boyfriend - yeah, it’s as convoluted as it sounds. The characters are all walking clichés. Daphne, on the other hand, dishes out some practical advice for the love-struck: “No matter how much you love someone, don’t lose yourself. Keep your own friends, hobbies, and alone time. can cringe be addictive????? This book was… a cringe-filled experience. Honestly, I went in with very low expectations, because the author’s most recent books have been a complete mess for me. And while this one wasn’t great, I have to admit: I devoured it. I couldn’t put it down. That addictive quality is the only reason it’s getting 2 stars instead of 1. Let’s get it straight—the characters? Absolutely unbearable. Cringe to the max. There’s even an entire chapter dedicated to the funeral of a goldfish… and I swear that scene is burned into my memory forever (for all the wrong reasons). I disliked every single character, and that’s me being kind. Then there were the flashbacks. Supposedly they were meant to help us understand the whole story, but they added nothing. I don’t need recycled flashbacks and recycled scenes. I want something new, something different. Is that really too much to ask? The plot itself was so fucking Predictable. I know, I know. Everyone loves Ann Patchett, just as everyone in this novel loves Joe and Sebastian and Lara and Ken and Maisie and the farm. Also Joe and Lara's three daughters, and the dog, and the grandmother. Also cherry pie. But a pile of comfy pillows only makes a nice place to read a good novel; it does not make an actual good novel. What happened to Ann Patchett's spice? To the rivalry and ambition and cunning and pain of her great novels like "Commonwealth," "The Dutch House," and"The Magician's Assistant"? In a word, this book is boring. Here's the plot, such as it is: As Covid spreads across the US in 2020, Joe and Lara are quarantining with their three grown daughters on the Michigan cherry farm that's been in Joe's family for generations. Without ordinary entertainment, this becomes a good time (supposedly) for Lara to tell the girls the story of her long-ago summer romance with Peter Duke, who later became a famous actor. That's the first problem: Since the daughters have spent their lifetimes repeatedly hearing that story and picking apart all the bits -- the eldest, Emily, is convinced that Duke is actually her father-- what's left for Lara to tell them? In order for this phony structure to work, someone has to constantly be saying: "I can't believe I never asked you that before." But the worse problem is that everyone is soooo loving and understanding. Joe isn't jealous of the focus on Duke. Lara doesn't regret giving up the lights and glory of her own acting career or the potential of sharing Duke's. The sisters exhibit no sibling rivalry. No one argues or disagrees, except occasionally in cute and minor ways. The sole narrative tension is whether they'll get all the cherries harvested in time. True, there's a good plot twist a bit more than halfway through, plus a few more twists after that (several of them eminently foreseeable and one totally unbelievable). But that's a long time to ask the reader to maintain interest. I didn't.

Rare occasion where the audiobook is better than the text Yep, scandalous I know, but I am going to share my disappointments about a book set largely in Michigan. Buckle up. During the pandemic, mother Laura/Lara sits down with her three adult daughters, sharing glimpses of the one summer Lara dated Peter Duke, a now famous movie star. The framing of this story is enormously too heavy. There is a now and then timeline, but the book spends too much time on the present timeline. The tone is a bit nauseating, a mixture of extreme sugary sweet with a melancholy sadness of regret and nostalgia for times past. And, the ending, although unexpected, seemed abrupt and dissatisfying. What happened to Pallace? Hasn’t Ann Patchett heard of Josephine Baker? On a bright note, the audiobook narrator, Meryl Streep, gave a wonderous performance! This was disappointing. I have enjoyed other books about Gabriel Allon, the spymaster for Israel, but this one was almost a DNF. Parts were simply not believable; other parts felt like they were pasted in. This reads like the last of a series.

The Daniel Silva works featuring Gabriel Allon are usually a joy to read. In addition to a masterfully designed plot and crackling suspense, the books offer much more. There is Historical information, there are Travelogues, lovingly detailed bits about art and music. Usually there are even enticing passages about food and wine that stir the readers senses. For much of The CELLIST this wonderful formula was repeated. We were treated to the reappearance of many of the Series most memorable characters and to a riveting story. However, the final portion of the book ( I understand Mr Silva has said he rewrote the ending), veered off into being like one of the shrill and boring Cable News “ Talking Heads” panels full of self virtuous, sanctimonious and biased analysis of the news and political scene. Mr Silva should have spared his fans of the Series his ramblings and left his wildly speculative diatribe to a New York Times Op-Ed piece. Such poorly connected logic was way beneath the mind of Gabriel Allon. The author spins his rationale for all this in his “Afterword “ but that too is a partisan cherry picking of facts to buttress a weak attempt at Virtue Signaling. All that made this ( indeed it has been a trend lately in the series) a disappointing effort to say the least

So many conflicting thoughts on this one. Silva concedes that he re-wrote much of the book in light of the 2020 election, transition, and events of January 6 (2021, of course). Since there isn't much middle ground as to how one views that period and those events, my guess is most folks will either appreciate it or be incensed by it. (For example, if you're a Q follower, you believe the election was "stolen," and you consider the community of January 6 "tourists" to be freedom fighters committed to preserving (their admittedly self-serving vision) of the Republic, I expect you'll be personally insulted by much of the book. If you fall into this category, I'd strongly encourage you to skip this one.) What's more difficult to assess is, say, you perceive the election was valid and you believe that those who stormed the Capitol belong in jail, then the issue is whether the book strikes too close to home or whether the reason you read Silva (and this type of stuff) generally, is for an escape, in which case, the book is as depressing as reading the newspaper each morning, so it's not as much fun as it might have been. If not, you might find the rapid pivot and "historical fiction" aspects hugely entertaining. For me, the error (mine, not the author's) lies in continuing to read this series during the pandemic/quarantine, when I don't spend the kind of time I normally would in steel tubes (planes & trains) and hotels. I got hooked on the series as a travel serial, the kind of thing I could read when trapped in place, often jet lagged, and, frankly, killing time. And I particularly enjoyed the action in countries and cities where I'd spent a fair amount of time ... and even the DC/Langley stuff is in my neighborhood. (But, in particular, it was fun reading one of the Vatican-based books while briefly working in Rome.) Sadly, I've found the later books - read in the comfort of my home - disappointing. While I concede I find the level of (canned) repetition frustrating, I can't even put my finger on it - they just haven't really worked for me. Are money laundering and political destabilization less entertaining than Middle Eastern murder and mayhem? I dunno. But this one dragged for me.... Hopefully, by the time the next one comes out, I'll be back on the road again.

** spoiler alert ** Ok, this one has me scratching my head. I chose to read this piece of nonsense based on the myriad 5-star reviews on Amazon—I’m talking HUNDREDS. Now there are two reasons this novel may have so much positive feedback. First, it could be that there are hundreds of readers who don’t often step beyond this author’s normal genre (of which this book did not belong) and are simply ride-or-die fans. Second, it could be that I’ve gone round the twist and am missing the value. I’m betting on the former. The writing here is, admittedly, pretty amazing. What is ludicrous, however, is the plot itself. **SPOILER ALERT AHEAD** Verity is a well-known and well liked author with a huge fan base. She and her husband lose their young twin girls some months apart in separate tragedies, then Verity herself is in a car accident. The accident leaves her in a semi-vegetative state, unable to move or communicate. Her husband seeks to hire an author to finish the last three books his wife had promised as part of a series of nine. In steps Lowen, a talented author in her own right, though certainly not as famous as Verity. She travels to the couple’s home, where Verity is under constant care (fed, diapered, etc.), in order to look over the woman’s notes in preparation for the writing Lowen has been commissioned to complete. Whilst rummaging through Verity’s office, and falling in love with Verity’s husband, Lowen discovers a manuscript that is supposedly an autobiography written by Verity before her accident. It is beyond disturbing and paints the now comatose author as a raging psychopath who despised her twins, feeling only raging jealousy at the attention they garner from their father. She has been cleaned, turned and fed and NO ONE KNEW? Additionally, we are to believe that she wrote the most disturbing things about herself and her children and labeled the manuscript an autobiography as a WRITING EXERCISE? What woman writes that she tried to abort her own children with a coat hanger as part of an exercise?? I could go on and on but I think you get the picture. Absurd is the only word that adequately conveys the entire premise. I wish someone, anyone, would have said to this author, “hey, you’re damn good, but this story just doesn’t make an iota of sense.” I’m left wishing back the hours it took me to read this insanely ridiculous drivel. Two stars for the obvious talent, but nless you are a die-hard fan of this writer, I’d skip this one altogether.

For example, she really write some weird awkward sentences… (1) “I know the radiation has already gotten through the tear in my body’s Hazmat.” (2) “He doesn’t have a brain below the waist.” (3) “They are the sorts of parents I have only read about in books. Tweedy and kind. I can’t understand how they raised such a horrible cow.” (4) “Jonas watches as I stroke Peter’s skin.” Is “stroke” the right word for applying sunscreen? (5) “Wipe crumps of soil off the butt of my jean shorts.” (6) “Our illicit proximity thrills through me.” (7) “Thin rulers of gray light stripe my bedspread… “ (8) “Do you suppose this is where the marital bed was?” That’s a very common question for a 12 year old boy to ask, right? (9) “My hair smells of bonfire smoke and ketchup.” Ketchup? No explanation provided. (10) “All of a sudden his body slumps, as if the sharp blade of discovery has de-boned him.” (11) My mother’s cure for all woes: “If you’re feeling depressed, organize your underwear drawer.” (12) “My voice teeth against teeth.” What does that even mean???? (13) “There’s something about a white cat that revolts me - a ratlike porn-y quality.” What??? (14) “Hummingbirds drinking flower nectar with their needle-beaks” Awkward much? (15) “An egg-yolk sun rises out of the dense tree line like a hot air balloon” Make up your mind… egg yolk or hot air balloon. And there are many more… these are but a few of the gems. Next, the author seems to be overly interested in pee, peeing and piss in general. There are so many references to pee, plot points involving pee and people peeing in general. OK… I get it, people pee, but there is so much of it in this book… why??!! What is the point? Was there a point? Here are a few examples I noted… there are many more I promise you… (1) “Tears have dried in piss-thin icicles on my cheeks.” Piss-thin icicles? Is that a thing??? (2) “Mouse piss or the slow drip drip of their afterbirth.“ SIDE NOTE: There are also MULTIPLE references to mouse afterbirth in this book. I am thinking that mouse afterbirth must be extremely tiny… how does it drip drip? I don’t think I have ever seen a mouse afterbirth in my 51 years on this earth, yet our main character refers to it at least twice in two different sections of the book. And again I ask WHY??? Just trying to gross us out for some reason? (3) “I hope you explained to your young man that we don’t flush for pee.” (4) “Peeing on the beach sitting down is even better than peeing in the shower standing up.” Really? WTF? How is the relevant? (5) “I only need to pee, but I’m tempted to take a shit in the toilet just to make a point.” What point can be made this way? How will the person in question know you’ve even done this? (6) “I have no choice but to sit down and pee with Gina two feet away, underpants around my ankles… “ There’s more, but I didn’t note it all down (yes, there’s even a “meet cute” scene where our main character pees in the street in front of her future husband shortly after they meet. How romantic! 💦) She also likes to name drop unusual product names for no apparent reason… (1) Leica camera (2) Hu-Kwu tea (3) Metrecal (4) Rothman cigarettes (5) Linguiça (6) Lanz Nightgowns (7) Medaglia d'Oro Italian Roast Espresso Instant Coffee (8) Sea Monkeys She loves WASP’y character names. (1) Wallace (2) Eleanor (3) Dixon (4) Whitman (5) Jonas (6) Conrad (7) Nanette (8) Austin And speaking of characters, there’s not a character in the entire book you can bond with or even like very much. Both of the romantic interests (Jonas & Peter) are DUDS. And finally after 386 pages there’s also an ambiguous ending which I won’t reveal here. So, if you’ve read this far, please take my word for it and don’t bother renting a room for even a single day in this shabby Paper Palace… the accommodations are “piss poor,” the staff won’t get you anywhere worth going and you will be lost in double quick time. Final word: Don’t believe the 5-star reviews.

This is Paula Hawkins third novel. The first one – “The Girl on the Train” was a runaway bestseller and a suspenseful, tense, and mesmerizing read. The second one – “Into the Water” – was a lesser quality follow-up that had too many points-of-view, discombobulating the complex story. This one – “A Slow Fire is Burning” – unfortunately leans more towards the weaknesses of her second book rather than the simple strengths of her first one. “A Slow Fire Burning Fire” starts off with the murder of a young man, Daniel Sutherland, whose body is discovered in a London houseboat. When the investigation begins, there are several potential suspects, including: Laura Kilbride - a troubled young lady with social challenges, who had a questionable one-night-stand with Daniel and was last seen leaving his houseboat the night previous to his murder. Carla Myerson – Daniel’s aunt, dealing not only with Daniel’s death, she is still recovering from the recent death of Daniel’s own mother and her sister. Theo Myerson – Carla’s ex-husband, who still shares an on and off relationship with her, is struggling with his writing career and jealousies. Miriam Lewis - a nosy neighbor who has a houseboat close to Daniel’s and seems to know a lot about him, as well as Laura’s troubled past and Theo’s writing sources too. Each of these four had their own personal connections to the victim and the secrets that included. Could one of them been harboring thoughts of revenge? Could that person be capable of killing? As the title suggests, is it possible that one those fires slowly burning has exploded in an act of madness and murder? When I was reading this book, it didn’t take me long to realize that it really felt like I was reading a Shari Lapena suburban mystery rather than the Paul Hawkins untrustworthy narrator point-of-view style that she so creatively developed in his first outing. I realize that this avenue of thought will not sit well with some readers and I understand that. It is not my intent to criticize any author or their works. However, having read all of Lapena’s novels, as well as Hawkins, this was a Lapena book in all of the key elements. Characters that were weak, flawed, and detached from reality as they try to overcome the negative influence of prior traumas. Plotting that involved a current murder mystery while moving back and forth in time to fill in back stories and secrets that each primary character is carrying. And the kicker that really makes it a Lapena product is that none of the characters (except for maybe Irene) are likeable. Not at all. They are strange and full of dark idiosyncrasies that make them interesting, but not sympathetic. Almost the whole time I was reading this book, I kept thinking is this Lapena writing or Hawkins? Or is it Hawkins writing a tribute to Lapena? I am sorry, but I couldn’t help it. Now, the real question after that becomes, was it good? For me, the answer is a bit yes, but mostly no. Yes, in that I liked how Hawkins moved back and forth between the various characters, as well as mixing in their past to link everything together. Most of the time she pulled this off in a smooth and somewhat seamless manner that delivered an additional depth to the various plotlines and character behaviors. However, I found the inserts of Theo’s mystery novel between the chapters to be distracting and annoying. Maybe that’s me, but I didn’t find them helpful. It felt like they were included to increase the page count beyond the 300 -page mark. No, for the primary reasons that I already stated (making me feel like I was reading a Lapena book). I wasn’t as interested as I wanted to be in watching each of the characters suffer psychological self-breakdowns, mostly driven by their own weaknesses and stupidity. I also found myself conflicted in that Hawkins had a lot going on with each of her characters, and at times it made the novel strong and interesting. However, at other times, it came across as a bit messy and convoluted in the delivery. I almost needed a scorecard to keep up with the activities. I understand that the current trend of psychological mysteries focuses on untrusty character viewpoints and building up to big twists and surprises at the end. Those can be incredibly hard to conceive and deliver in an exceptional manner. It takes superb plotting in which the clues, red herrings, and critical information is doled out slowly at key moments throughout as the author builds to a big and shocking climax. Characters must be fleshed out enough to be interesting and captivating, carrying secrets and demonstrating dark behaviors. Anyone who can pull that off successfully has my full respect. Hawkins uses her title to create multiple storylines that examine people dealing with real and personal problems, creating a slow burning fire within them, building in fury throughout the book, and finally combusting at the end in tragic and revealing ways. However, as well as it may have been conceived and constructed, Hawkins falls short on the execution and delivery. The first 200 pages take a long time to get going, and then the last 100 pages didn’t really provide an emotional payoff. Again, maybe it’s me, but I not only figured out who the killer was early in the book, I also nailed the reason for him/her committing the murder. Even with all that Hawkins had going on, it still felt predictable. My primary struggles were the same that I have with Lapena; although the characters are interesting, they are not sympathetic or empathetic in almost every way. There is no one to cheer for, no one to really draw on and emotionally care about and invest my attention on. It’s like flipping through the channels and hitting on an old Jerry Springer episode where the guests are so unrelatable that you aren’t rally invested in their outcomes. That’s the same here. Interesting, obnoxious, and dysfunctional in a trashy way, but not necessarily memorable. Overall, this was not bad, but not as good as it could have been either. I wanted to like it. I truly did. But the truth is, it just didn’t provide the level of excitement that I was hoping for as I plodded through it, hoping it would get better. It just felt like it could have been better, as if Hawkins was trying to do too much and it showed at times, and not relying enough on what her own strengths really are. Here’s to hoping for a better outcome next time…

Another Entry Showing How This Once Great Series Has Lost Its Edge! With An Inside Job, Silva delivers yet another polished entry in the Gabriel Allon series — but also another highly formulaic and somewhat stale reminder of how far the books have drifted from what made them compelling in the first place; especially in the last four books. Early Allon novels crackled with urgency: morally complex geopolitics, genuine tradecraft, emotional stakes rooted in Gabriel’s past, and a constant sense of danger. Here, that tension is mostly muted. The plot leans heavily on the now-familiar formula — assemble the elite team, follow cultured breadcrumbs through Europe, resolve the crisis with near-effortless precision. The unpredictability and raw edge that once defined the series have been replaced by a smoother, safer, much more predictable rhythm. Further, Gabriel himself has evolved from a haunted, conflicted intelligence operative into something closer to an untouchable master problem-solver. The vulnerability and moral weight that once gave his victories meaning, and which caused his personal life to be so conflicted, are largely absent. Without that friction, the story reads more like a well-produced procedural than a high-stakes thriller. Silva remains a skilled craftsman, and the novel is readable; but also one that becomes forgettable right after finishing it. For a reader such as myself who has read all 25 books in this series, I’ve become beyond disappointed with how the series has stepped away from the very qualities — grit, risk, emotional depth — that made it a standout in modern espionage fiction. As I said in previous reviews, it’s time for Silva to let Allon REALLY retire and for himself to step outside of the Comfort Zone he’s been in for much too long and create a new series with new, fresh characters and new, fresh plots. Since I just learned that Silva has a new Gabriel Allon book due out on July 14th, titled Ransom, my hope for a new series is dashed. I guess it’s understandable why Silva won’t do this, at least any time soon, since the series is too much of a “cash cow” for him to give it up.

A political diatribe masquerading as thriller fiction. Coulnd't finish it. The other 19 Gabriel Allon stories were all excellent.

Silva, whom I used to really like, is phoning it in. From the GR rating, I can see I'm the only one who thinks so. Here, Allon is vacationing in Venice when the Vatican calls for his assistance again. The current Pope has died from his third heart attack in six months; obviously that's suspicious. Naturally, they call the head of Israeli Intelligence to investigate. That's the job of Israeli Intelligence, to investigate, pro bono, unlikely crimes that have nothing to do with Israel, right? But wait: it does have something to do with Israel. Turns out the Pope died right after finding a [Roman] document from the time of Christ, Pontius Pilate's confession. Yay! This will expose anti-Semitism as the product of a Vatican/Roman spin campaign--they blamed the Jews, and really, it was always the Romans who killed Christ. This is the interesting point in the book--does all anti-Semitism grow from the Christian notion that Jewish leaders induced the Romans to kill Christ? Perhaps it does. But a 2,000 year-old revelation isn't going to change that. So the Allon investigation goes in the usual, invented-by-a-six-year-old way. They look for a conspiracy, and immediately find it. The hack the phone of a conspirator, and know everything: who's in on it, how much money they were paid, where it comes from, what the goals are. A twenty-seven-year-old hacker, living in her parent's basement, could defeat the forces of evil if it were this easy. The conspirators have bought the votes of a bunch of cardinals to fix the election of the next Pope. Now that Allon knows all, he can destroy the conspiracy. Come on, Silva, really. The bad guys went from Cardinal to Cardinal and said, "Pssst. Wanna make some major cash? Here's who you vote for, next time there's a conclave." Let's say that would work a few times. Let's say, with unlimited funds, you could buy a bunch of cardinals. Did they have a 100% success rate? Because if they asked just one cardinal who refused, just one cardinal who was not willing to betray the church, his faith, his God, and his principles, then he blows the whistle and the scheme collapses. Which brings me to my joke headline from a month ago, when the real Pope was visiting Baghdad: 'Pope takes opportunity in Baghdad to issue fatwa against U.S. plaintiff's bar.' The book is plodding, uninspiring, unworthy. Even the prose is lazy: lots and lots of telling, where Allon and others allegedly feel emotions, but we don't see them. And his dialogue might as well all be from the same character: it's all in the same style. Silva's style of dialogue: 'I finished it." "Finished what?" "The book." "How was it?" "It had its moments." "Such as?" "I liked the ending." And so on. EVERY CHARACTER speaks evasively, as though the author had paid him to avoid revealing any information as long as possible. This is not tension-building; this is lame.

Off Course In The Order Silva drifts from international thriller to a thinly veiled political treatise. Espionage operations and action scenes lack the depth of previous Gabriel Allon adventures. Having read every Silva novel, The Order is the only one that was time wasted. It reads more like a NY Times opinion piece than spy thriller.

Predictable I have read all of Silva's books, many several times. His later novels have become too predictable and uninspiring. The Order was more of a chore to read, rather than a joy to read.

★★☆☆☆ 2/5 “Some of us just want to fuck with your feelings, not burn your house to the ground.” ✎ (❁ᴗ͈ˬᴗ͈) ༉ Note : This review contains major plot spoilers. Please read at your own risk. I strongly advise you to not read this review if you haven't read the book and are planning to. Onyx Storm is the third installment of five in The Empyrean series. It picks up a time after the ending of Iron Flame, and follows Violet through her tumultuous journey. I most definitely went into this book with expectations higher than I should've, especially considering nearly every single one of them was met with utter disappointment. I will not be breaking down the characters and instead will make this one lengthy review because I have a lot of opinions, many of them not amazing. Let's get started. Just to preface one more time—there are spoilers in this review for both characters and plot. Please do not read if you plan to read the book on your own time, are reading it now, or plan to read it in the future. : ̗̀➛ My Review Rants “You named a kitten Broccoli?” “No one really wants broccoli, but it's good for you, so seems fitting to me.” To start off this review, let's start with the pacing of this book—which was atrocious. Iron Flame ended with one of the most interesting plotlines we could have received in this series, and this book just didn't hold that plotline up well enough. We jump into this one with an already established time jump, and then another following it, with unsubstantial information on what is happening in the world or to Xaden. We spent far too long of the beginning of this book still at Basgiath dealing with political issues that genuinely made no sense. It honestly felt as if Basgiath's higher chain of command wanted to cause an inner war outside of the venin already hunting them down over. . . fliers. Over people who quite literally saved their asses. We spent around 15% of this book following Violet fighting to choose her own hand-selected team for a top priority mission—find Andarna's family, the seventh dragon breed. Only, she never gets to choose her own team. She is put under the command of a man she hates and in a team she cannot trust. Sure, it happens. But we spent so long in the book following Violet argue to get her own team only for this entire team to die in less than a chapter in the most overly dramatic, nonsensical way you would almost think we were reading about toddlers drawing on the walls with crayons than military trained soldiers. And then after 20% of the book focusing on this, now Violet gets to handpick her team. Seems a bit redundant to spend so much time with Violet fighting for this just to have it resolved in less than a chapter, doesn't it? Then the only part of the book that I enjoyed—traveling to the other countries. This was roughly another 40% of the book and was genuinely the most interesting part of it. I may be the only one who feels this way, but if this is going to be a 5-book series, I would've preferred this book focusing on this travel only the entire time because it was NOT fleshed out enough. Violet finally gets her team together - herself, Xaden, Cat, Garrick, Ridoc, Trager, Maren, Dain, and the crown prince, Halden (who is eventually changed out for Aaric). Mission: find the irid dragons, Andarna's family, and also learn more from Violet's father, Asher. Except everything her father leaves is cryptid and annoyingly tedious to deal with. It gives us the feeling of learning more about him, the way he lived and loved, and the travels he went on. Except we don't actually learn that much about him or who he was before passing away. Then we learn more about Violet's childhood, how she was nearly dedicated to a temple of Dunne and is why she has partially silver hair. But a lot of this knowledge is so sporadic and not nearly as delved or fleshed into because we are given no time to explore it in this book before moving on. We are basically dripfed information in small, not at all appealing ways. How ridiculous. I do feel the focus on Andarna's emotional stability was interesting, one of the more enjoyable parts of the book, but it wasn't fleshed out enough. We should have gotten to know more about her emotional wellbeing, her mental state after being rejected by her family beyond just - oh, Andarna is sad. She is heartbroken. There was so much going on in this book and none of them were executed well. Political upheaval in Basgiath, the irids, finding a cure for Xaden, Violet's father's books, Violet's childhood, Xaden's mother (which, why was she so important while they were there, but then never mentioned again by any characters afterwards?
