(Vague Spoilers) Unpopular Opinion Time! I love the Stormlight Archive, but I have numerous issues with this book. I believe that Rhythm of War will be known as “the Slog” of the Stormlight Archive, similar to the infamous lull in the middle of Wheel of Time. And while this is a great Cosmere novel, it is the weakest Stormlight Archive installment to date. It’s also the bleakest of the series, and hard to read at times. THE GOOD New POV’s: We get numerous new POV characters, of which the two most important are Navani Kholin and Venli. Of the two, Navani’s story is by far the more interesting. She takes center stage for the majority of the book, and finds new confidence in herself as she struggles with a complicated relationship with one of the Fused. That entire storyline is entertaining, even if an important discovery she makes seems a bit... questionable. Hopefully the next book will clarify. Character Growth: by the end of the book, we finally get some important character growth for both Kaladin and Shallan that's we've been waiting a loooooong time for. The down side is things get worse for both characters before they get better, and the book drags because of it. Cosmere Heavy: considering some of the books shortcomings (outlined below), it seems like the author tried to keep the fans attention by making this the single most Cosmere-centric book he’s written so far. The Cosmere revelations come early and often, which is great, except... THE NOT-SO-GOOD ...the book is SO Cosmere heavy that anyone not following the overall Cosmere story will be confused as hell. The author has stated that you should be able to pick up any of his Cosmere books and read them independently from the other series, but anyone not familiar with Cosmere lore will be either confused or feel they are missing part of the story. At the least, you’ll need to have read Elantris, Mistborn Era 1, Warbreaker, his White Sand graphic novels, and the Dawnshard novella to really understand what’s going on. I also found the Cosmere reveals to be very “info-dumpy”. The author just gave a wink at the audience and said “here you go Cosmere fans!” No “Sanderlanches”: or rather, a mini Sanderlanche at the beginning, and one at the very end. Everything else is slooooooow going. The gradual build up to a sustained and exciting ending that we’ve come to expect from SA books didn’t really happen here. Inconsistent: the story is all over the place. Past books had more consistent slow build plot progressions, but this book was very disjointed, jumping from character to character seemingly at random. It made for a schizophrenic reading experience. Taravangian: the author tipped his hand early in this book, and I saw where Taravangian’s story was headed. Unfortunately, while it was interesting, I feel like he is acting very out of character at the end of the book. Predictable: Taravangian’s wasn’t the only story that was a foregone conclusion; almost every storyline in the book was predictable (Kaladin’s, Shallon’s, Vinli’s, Navani’s - all predictable) and there was a long wait to finally get to the payoffs that you knew were coming. Flashbacks: Venli is the character who’s past is the subject of this books flashbacks, and by and large were not really needed, as almost nothing was new information. It felt like filler, though her story in the present was more interesting. Speaking of Vinli... Vinli: I just don't find her to be a likable character. And we spend an unfortunate amount of time with Vinli in this book. THE BAD Religious Agenda: I get shouted down often for griping about the authors religious agenda. Religion is always a major theme in nearly all of Sanderson’s books, with varying degrees of overtness. There’s really no denying it was there in this book. Navani has a very low moment and prays to god for help. Even though she knows he’s dead, she “keeps the faith”, and the moment she prays for help she’s instantly given the perfect solution to her problems. My eyes rolled so hard they nearly fell out of my head. This isn’t the first time the author has played the “pray and receive instant miracle” card either. Wouldn’t it be great if in real life you got instant miracles the moment you have a crisis of faith? Lazy writing, with a ham-fisted religious message. Jasnah: the best character in the Cosmere for me is Jasnah, and we still get extremely minimal screen time with her. The scant few POV moments we get with her we are treated to an implication that she’s not very interested in physical intimacy. I’ve long worried that Jasnah may be used as a means of taking cheap shots at atheism. So far I haven’t detected any overt attempts to do so, but implying she’s too logical to enjoy sex does nothing to increase my confidence. THE VERDICT I still love the Stormlight Archives, and I did enjoy the book overall, but Rhythm of War was a big dip in quality over previous books. I have hope that Sanderson will turn things around in book five.

** spoiler alert ** This is... most certainly a book. A good book. A good, long book. I feel many will like it, many will love it. I am not one of those people. This book exposes the one chink in brandon's armor, the one weakness in his otherwise brilliant and commendable writing style, drive, and ambition. It highlights a concern that I've harbored for a time, but more on that later. First, I want to give this book its due praise. It consists of pretty much everything you might look for in a Sanderson book. We've got characters that are not only deep and interesting, but fun to read about. We have a superb world, built to hold under 'scientific' scrutiny. And of course we can't forget about the Sanderlanche, which made me write this review under the influence of sleep depravity, as i could not put it down until 3 am. I don't want to dive deeper into what made this book good, because those praises are very predictable, having been said a thousand times over. This book will arrive to the destination you expect it to get to, but as many characters are so fond of saying in this series; journey before destination. The journey in this case has exactly what you expect it to have, all the twists and turns in the road we have all became fond of. It makes the book predictable. Not quite boring, just unsatisfying and much less interesting. The strife of some characters, mainly Shallan and Kaladin just feel like they are going through the motions. Again. Collectively, at this point, the series consists of over four thousand pages. Each of these characters have gotten more page space than most main characters in more traditional fantasy stories. Those two have made a step forward, yes, they've been transformed. But every book seems like they make two steps forward and one step back. That's technically moving forward, but I have personally felt so fatigued and fed up with them that... I just didn't care as much anymore. Yes, in real life depression and DID doesn't just go away like that and their experience in this series is a realistic one. But there's a reason why fiction doesn't follow its real life examples to the letter. I can very much appreciate what Sanderson did and does for the depiction of mental illnesses for and in the fantasy community, as it expands the boundary of fantasy and with it, human imagination. It begs the question though, if this dynamic shifting back and forth, the struggle these characters show with their mental states, if it becomes constant and viewed over a longer period of time, does it not become monotone? A single note, played until it has far since overstayed its welcome? There is a way Sanderson could overcome this obstacle. The old nihilistic adage of what doesn't kill me makes me stronger, only applies as long as what doesn't kill me doesn't break me, as well. That is something Sanderson makes apparent not only through Kaladin, but the heralds and the Fused as well. And they are broken, but these heroes persist despite it all. They are in a way such traditional heroes, that their struggle feels like there are no stakes to them. I was never afraid for any of the characters, my lethargy to their conflicts was so strong that i couldn't even muster an eye roll at the predictable path and resolution they were walking towards. Navani is a bondsmith, no duh. The tower will survive, no duh. Kaladin will survive and regain his strength, saving the day, no duh. Shallan will stay, no duh. If Sanderson would kill of one of the main characters, or at least let Shallan leave, driving in the point above, it would build up the stakes to a similar height that they were in Oathbringer. Though I suspect that was never the point of this book, i feel it will be a big hurdle in the future because that d0es make the book boring. So what is the point of the book? In my honest opinion, Sanderson has a vision for how he wants the first part of this series to end, but in order to achieve it he needs to have certain concepts explained. This book essentially contains a myriad of small info dumps and really make the world come together. I was grateful for this, at first, because he has always been excellent at worldbuilding and it is one of the best parts of SA, but it quickly felt undeserved and, for the most part, unimportant. Roshar is a planet, and there are other planets! And the characters are all like, wow, that's cool, it totally shatters my worldview, but then they proceed as if nothing has happened. This is why i think Shallan of all people should have left with the ghostbloods, because her curious nature combined with the pain from her past could and should have driven her towards them. It just feels so cliche to have her reject that offer and choose the side love and honor and be a good little girl that knows her place. It would have raised the stakes for other characters, showing that Sanderson isn't afraid to stray from his own mould. Instead she slips back into her own monotony, a little better, more complete as a person overall (literally, in her case), but that's more of a narrative trick at this point, than anything else. Speaking of which, i think it's really ironic how he has Hoid spouting off about doing the kansas city shuffle, but then refuses to do anything but the most obvious for all of the characters. Well, with the exception of one. This is of course entirely subjective and maybe I have in my love for Sanderson's work got to know and understand him, at least the writer part. And so i can anticipate his next move. Perhaps that is the burden of knowledge, losing the excitement fueled by curiosity of the unknown. Though I very much hope that, like the Fused, like Raboniel, I too will be surprised. On the other hand, however, there are certain things you might expect from Sanderson that just aren't here. There have been a few theories that people have gone mad over since Oathbringer. The two main ones that i remember the most are that the Sibling is of both honor and cultivation and that it resides in Urithiru, and that the fourth ideal gives access to shardplate. Both of these things are confirmed so anticlimactically that i felt disappointed. Yes, Kaladin still has a pretty epic and emotional acquisition of it, but we all knew it was coming after it was so anticlimactically announced. I didn't expect Taravangian to become Odium. This is again very subjective but I didn't like that part. I mean, i did, i really did, but i didn't like how Rayse has been simply brushed off after three thousand pages, more, of building him up. Though I suppose the stakes have been raised because of it. It shows another problem that happens to a lot of characters where things just feel too convenient for them. From Adolin suddenly thinking of asking for a trial against the spren, to nightblood and taravangian being in the right spot at the right time. And i do understand that there are things involved here, like seeing the future and so on, but it just feels so damn convenient. Sanderson pretty much explains a lot of the world and the underlying principles of the cosmere, except the one that actually matters here, which is how was Taravangian able to draw nightblood without it killing him immediately AND transferring it into the spiritual realm to stab Rayse. It feels so fake to have both of these characters squirm and obsess with what they are going to do next, but then at the last moment they have this shining revelation. Which would be fine, except neither Adolin nor the sympathetic Taravangian fit this character type. Despite the fact that i stayed glued to the page for the last part of the book, I felt that Sanderson has been emotionally manipulating me, showing me the things I want to see, giving me my destination, but the journey felt empty. You can't spend time with characters and not care about them for this long, but this feels more like an old ex trying to play on your emotions to lure you into their embrace, which might feel good for a time, but as soon as the infatuation wears out, you see them for their true, empty self. That is how i feel towards this book. I could go on with describing the sometimes awkward dialogue, but that would be nitpicking, i feel. Though i mention it to further support this next point. Even this awkward dialogue, usually between two people discussing something very personal and intimate, used to serve in Brandon's benefit. In Mistborn it was endearing and kind of cute. Here it's sloppy. Rushed. And that is my main gripe with this book and my main concern, as i mentioned in the first paragraph. This whole book feels like that. It isn't as tight as some of his other works, and considering its his latest, it should be pretty high up on the list. But it's not. Now, I'm not demanding perfection every time, as i feel Oathbringer has been. My concern stems from some of the things Sanderson has said previously as well as on the release party video you can find on his youtube channel. He said that for every story that he tells, there are a thousand that he won't get to. And i think that scares him. Or at least gives him some sort of anxiety. I wholeheartedly empathise and sympathise with him, but i fear its starting to show on his work. Dawnshard was sloppy. Rhythm of War was sloppy. And i can only hope that it's not because of some Brandon's inner termoil, but because of outstanding circumstances. Such as covid-19. He has said that his team worked very hard to get this out this soon, and maybe they got a bit sloppy too. Maybe his speed of writing is making him rush to finish it and as many other stories as he possibly can. I think his team is both an asset and a hindrance for his works, because he is suddenly dependent on them to tell a good story. We have seen something like this influence his writing before, like when he postponed the continuation of Mistborn in favor of Skyward, because he wanted to give his other publisher something to publish. This is something that has been seen time and time again, mostly with big corporations, that as your influence expands you start to become dependent on other people, you start surrendering your power to them. I feel its unfair that Brandon gets all the love for the stories he writes, despite the fact that he does try very hard to get the people who have worked WITH him on them to get some of the recognition. But the more popular he gets, the bigger his team will get and his dependence on their performance increases. If he does not keep a tight grip on the reins, both for his team and for himself, i feel the coming stories will just get sloppier and more rushed. That is not to say that i think this more collective way of producing stories is wrong, quite the opposite. But it comes with a set of weaknesses as well, which one should be mindful of. All in all, I can not see into the future but only speculate on it, and in this world i have seen this same spiraling pattern too many times. Perhaps, and i hope that it will, my pessimism will hold no ground, but that is also the reason why i'm writing this long essay on the subject. I am eager to look at it in the future, seeing how my concerns held up. Perhaps this book is, at least to me, going to be a black sheep, a necessary sacrifice to bring the first half of the series to its spectacular conclusion. Whatever the case may be, i look forward to the next installments and despite my bad rating, this is very obviously a must read for a cosmere/Sanderson fan, and it is despite all its shortcomings, still a very good book. But it's just not a very good Sanderson book.

One of the most boring books I’ve read. A textbook with dialogue. I’ve given it two stars because it’s well written and follows Sandford’s basic plotting system — i.e., the reader knows who the criminals are from the beginning, and the cops do too. Over the past three years, Bill Clinton and James Patterson have developed a bankable formula: In their previous thriller, a U.S. president went missing. In their new thriller, a president’s daughter goes missing. If this keeps up, someday we’ll have to read a thriller about the president’s lost cat, his missing keys, an errant sock. And why not? “The President Is Missing” was the best-selling novel of 2018, demonstrating that, as in politics, nothing sells like name recognition. Tellingly, “The President’s Daughter” opens with a shout-out to Washington super-agent Robert Barnett, who convinced these two American brands they could cash in yet again. It’s the economy, stupid. Readers expecting a sequel, though, will discover that this new novel offers an entirely different cast of characters. “The President Is Missing” gave us President Jonathan Lincoln Duncan, a former Gulf War hero who battles a dastardly terrorist. But “The President’s Daughter” gives us President Matthew Keating, a former Navy SEAL hero who battles a dastardly terrorist. It’s a change as startling as the shift from tan to beige. With this brave and monogamous hero, Clinton has once again revealed such a naked fantasy version of himself that you almost feel embarrassed for the man. And that’s pretty much where the revelations peter out. The publishers claim that Clinton has contributed information that could be provided only by a former president — or, I would add, by somebody who’s. . . . I consumed this as an audio book on a family road trip. As I write this, the former Navy SEAL who shot bin Laden has just gone on a talk show to say that he could have gotten all the Americans out of Afghanistan with just nine guys. They'd kill every Taliban in Kabul, and bring all the Americans home. This is pretty much the tone of The President's Daughter, where the daughter of a former president is kidnapped by an Islamist Terrorist. The ex-President, who doesn't let a chapter go by without reminding us he's a former SEAL, becomes fed up with the ulterior motives of his backstabbing, politically-motivated successor. So he assembles a Band-of-Brothers (and one Sister) to--in defiance of the current president--infiltrate Libya, kill the bad guys, and rescue his daughter. It's a love letter to militarism, cutting through red tape with an automatic weapon, and the moral superiority of elite soldiers over politicians. It's casually racist and sexist, but its protagonists would laugh at that criticism, because they know how the world REALLY works, and true nobility is recognized among the warrior cast and those who adore them. It seems like a right-wing fantasy, but as the SEAL on the talk show might point out, what would a person like ME know about what's fact versus fantasy on the ground in Afghanistan. And surely the reason we spent 20 fruitless years there was because of bad political leadership. Or something. As with Patterson's last "collaboration" with former President Bill Clinton, the latter's contribution appears to be a statesmanly speech at the end (in this case, a Presidential transition letter) that has no bearing on the story. As for the story... I could describe how the writing was silly and ham-fisted, but who am I to criticize an author worth $800 million? The chapters are short, and each ends with a mini cliffhanger, pulling you through. It's written for short attention spans, so the main ideas are explained and re-explained. The details practically scream "and this is where I did my research with sources Who Know, so let me info-dump!" Even if you're laughing or cringing, you want to see how it ends.

Hats off to Mr. Patterson for the longer bio at the back of the book than the former president. That speaks to his prolificness and promotional skills (the latter from his time on Madison Avenue no doubt). He sure pumps them out. I would love to know how many words he and Former President Clinton actually wrote. That silly carping aside, let me get down to the real carping. I did enjoy Patterson’s earliest work until he became a factory sped along by co-writers and collaborators. His strength is in concept, not execution. I found recent efforts to be more like graphic novels without the graphics. The President’s Daughter reads like a teenager’s video game. You know, it is actually YA now that I think of it. Patterson certainly knows his audience. This book zings along like a watered-down Tom Clancy but is so pedantically written, that unlike Clancy, you do not need to remember the character’s names. The chapters are never more than a handful of pages. In terms of plot and characters, Patterson reminds the reader of each so often that the most distracted or addled can easily follow along. So much so, that you could read to the halfway mark, wait ten years, pick it up and keep going without missing a beat like a See the President Run book. I found the reminders boring, repetitive and demeaning. If it was kept tight and gave the reader some credit, a hundred pages could be lopped. I really felt bad for how women came off in the book. The former president’s wife has a couple of good scenes but seems totally detached from everything. It would have had made more sense if she was no longer in the picture. The current female president is a vacuous sub-villainess with no claws. There are a couple of supporting female characters but they are completely one-dimensional caricatures. Some heft is given to the book's namesake but it does not make up for the overall impression. The men are little better, clocking in at one-point-five dimensional. Remember how for much of this century that Muslims were the new Nazis and Soviets? Well, here they are again completely misunderstood and given way too much weight in the grand game of geopolitics. There is a Chinese baddie who should get the main role but is a feint. If President Clinton doesn’t know Russia is the ultimate enemy, I’d be surprised. The worst criticism concerns a massive spoiler alert so do not continue if you intend to read the book. The president’s daughter should have remained offed. That was so silly, so trite, that I almost stopped reading. Not that I couldn’t predict the ending, I remained intrigued not for the story but to see how dumbed-down the whole thing was constructed. The ending pushed credibility further. American pluckiness, might and right prevails with absolutely no nod to the country’s real foreign policy. As the last pages wound down, I heard a mix of Lee Greenwood, the soundtrack to Team America, and Homer Simpson chanting, “USA, USA.”
